source.title_on_document: If ChatGPT can do it, where is my creativity? generative AI boosts performance but diminishes experience in creative writing

supplement.where: Appendix A. Supplementary data: online at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chbah.2025.100140 (p. 13)
supplement.holds: SI Table 1 (a detailed demographic breakdown; the paper does not say whether it gives arm sizes), SI Table 2 (ICC scores among all four raters), SI Table 3 (regressions of frequency, flexibility, inaccuracy, unclarity and writing time on condition, within each group and across groups), SI Table 4 (HAI dyad analysis), SI Table 5 (group-level creativity), SI Table 6 (perception regressions). The pooled across-group treatment effects appear only in SI Table 3. The main text prints Fig. 2 arm means with 95 percent CIs (no numbers) and b, SE and p for three within-group contrasts; arm sizes are not in the main text.

paper_design_summary: UK university students recruited on Prolific were first labelled into four groups by native English status and prior ChatGPT experience and then randomly assigned, between subjects, to an AI condition (asked to make sure they used ChatGPT) or a control condition (forbidden from using ChatGPT); of the 266 who completed the study, 43 failed an attention check and were excluded, leaving 225 analyzed. Each wrote a short piece (about 100 words, 10 minutes) describing as many uses as possible for a 'printer that can print anything in 2097'. An LLM validated against three human raters counted uses (fluency) and conceptual domains (flexibility) in each piece, the paper also reports both counts for each condition's pooled outputs, and Grammarly counted grammar errors and clarity suggestions; pre- and post-task perception surveys were also collected.

studies.label: Online experiment: printer-uses writing task with vs without ChatGPT

assignment.what_was_assigned: Condition: AI (participants 'were explicitly asked to make sure they used ChatGPT for the task') or Control ('forbidden from using ChatGPT for the task'). Participants were first labelled into four groups by English proficiency and prior ChatGPT experience; the paper says this 'ensured balanced representation across both control and experimental conditions' (p. 4) but does not say whether the randomization was stratified by group.
assignment.quote: After the pre-task survey, the experiment used a between-subjects design to randomly assign participants into one of two treatment conditions: the control condition (these participants were forbidden from using ChatGPT for the task)
assignment.locator: p. 5, Section 2.2 Design (continued), left column; also p. 4, Fig. 1 caption

arms.name: AI
arms.description: Participants were explicitly asked to make sure they used ChatGPT for the task and reported their ChatGPT usage afterwards. Self-reported usage: 27 percent relied entirely on ChatGPT, 47 percent made minor or major changes to the AI-generated output, 21 percent used their own prompts or a feedback loop, 5 percent unclassified (p. 6).

arms.name: Control
arms.description: Participants were forbidden from using ChatGPT for the task and reported any tool use afterwards; 90 percent reported using no digital tools (p. 6).

participants.exclusions: 266 participants completed the study; 43 who failed the attention check were excluded, 'leaving a final sample of 225' (p. 4). Random assignment followed the pre-task survey (p. 5), and the 43 had completed the study, so they were dropped after assignment. The paper does not say where in the study the attention check sat. The printed numbers do not close: 266 - 43 = 223, while the four group counts (58 + 60 + 54 + 53) sum to 225 (p. 4). The t-tests on p. 8 report t(221) for a within-person comparison and t(220) for Control vs AI, which imply 222 people for a paired and a two-sample Student t-test. The paper gives no count at assignment and no arm sizes in the main text. No intention-to-treat analysis is reported.
participants.who: Current students at a university in the United Kingdom, recruited via Prolific; mean age 29.07 (SD 8.59); 51 percent male, 48 percent female; 60 percent undergraduates, 31 percent postgraduates (including 13 PhD students). Four groups: Non-Native Inexperienced n = 58, Native Inexperienced n = 60, Non-Native Experienced n = 54, Native Experienced n = 53.
participants.quote: A total of 266 participants completed the study, all current students studying at a university in the United Kingdom. ... Forty-three people who failed the attention check were excluded from further analysis, leaving a final sample of 225.
participants.locator: p. 4, Section 2.1 Participants; group counts p. 4, Section 2.2 Design

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT. The paper does not state which model or tier participants used. It names GPT-4o and GPT-4 Turbo only as the models the researchers used to score the outputs (p. 5, Section 2.3).
ai_tool.how_used: AI-arm participants 'were explicitly asked to make sure they used ChatGPT for the task' (p. 5, Section 2.2). The paper reports no instruction on how to use it, and it does not say how participants reached ChatGPT. Self-reports: 27 percent relied entirely on ChatGPT, 47 percent made minor or major changes to its output, 21 percent used their own prompts or a feedback loop with ChatGPT, 5 percent unclassified (p. 6, Section 3.2.2).

task.description: Write a short piece (approx. 100 words) describing uses for a hypothetical 'printer that can print anything in 2097', instructed to 'describe as many unique uses as possible for this printer, AND do so as quickly as possible in 10 minutes' and to minimise grammar errors and maximise clarity. The paper calls it a creative writing task; it is scored like an alternate-uses test, for fluency and flexibility.

outcomes.name: Frequency (fluency): number of different uses of the printer in a participant's piece
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Uses counted by an LLM with a few-shot prompt (GPT4o and GPT4 Turbo, temperature 0); the paper does not say which model's counts enter the analysis. Validation: a random sample of 40 responses (5 from each group and condition) coded by three human raters from the research team, blinded to group and condition; average human ICC 0.81; human average vs GPT-4o ICC 0.93 for frequency (p. 5; four-rater ICCs in SI Table 2). Coded category_count because the score is a count of ideas; the counting was done by a language model, so automated_score is the alternative code.

contrasts.reported: Pooled across groups the text says AI participants had 'higher frequency and flexibility of creativity' (p. 6); the pooled regression is only in SI Table 3. Fig. 2 plots arm means with 95% CIs for each of the four groups, with no numbers printed; the AI mean is above Control in all four. Group 2 (Native, Inexperienced): 'no significant differences were observed for frequency (b = 0.91, SE = 2.30, p = .69)'. Group 4 (Native, Experienced): 'No significant differences were found in flexibility, correctness, frequency, or clarity'. Fig. 3 (p. 7) repeats the comparison in 21 demographic subgroups.
contrasts.locator: p. 6, Section 3.2 and Fig. 2; p. 7, Fig. 3; SI Table 3 (not in this PDF)

outcomes.name: Flexibility: number of unique conceptual domains represented by a participant's uses
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Domains counted by the same LLM procedure (GPT4o and GPT4 Turbo, temperature 0, few-shot). Example on p. 5: houses, villages and buildings give frequency 3 and flexibility 1. Average human ICC 0.81; human average vs GPT-4o ICC 0.83 for flexibility (p. 5). Section 2.3 glosses flexibility as 'variety/quality of ideas'; the Fig. 2 caption glosses it as 'numbers of unique uses'.

contrasts.reported: Text: AI participants had 'higher frequency and flexibility of creativity' (p. 6). Fig. 2 plots arm means with 95% CIs by group, with no numbers printed; the AI mean is above Control in all four groups. Group 4 (Native, Experienced): 'No significant differences were found in flexibility, correctness, frequency, or clarity'. No coefficient for flexibility is printed; the regressions are in SI Table 3. Fig. 3 (p. 7) repeats the comparison in 21 demographic subgroups.
contrasts.locator: p. 6, Section 3.2 and Fig. 2; p. 7, Fig. 3; SI Table 3 (not in this PDF)

outcomes.name: Group-level frequency: number of different uses, scored for each condition's pooled outputs (Fig. 5, bottom panel)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Frequency scored for 'collections of participants that share a characteristic or condition' (p. 7): one count per condition for all participants (Grp 9) and for eight subgroups (Grps 1-8). The paper does not describe the computation. The counts are not additive across subgroups (see diversity_detail.notes), so they are not plain sums of individual counts. The paper reports no scaling by arm size, and arm sizes are not in the main text. The paper reads the group-level results as evidence on the diversity of ideas (Section 4.2.3, p. 10).

eligibility.reason: Individuals were randomly assigned, between subjects, to use ChatGPT or not after the pre-task survey (p. 5; Fig. 1, p. 4), and the control arm was forbidden from using ChatGPT. The paper analyzed 225 people (p. 4), far above 50. The printed counts do not close (266 - 43 = 223, and the p. 8 t-tests imply 222 people), but every count clears 50 by a wide margin. Fluency and flexibility were counted on each written piece by an LLM validated against blinded human raters (p. 5), and the AI arm wrote with ChatGPT available. Arm sizes are not in the main text, and the pooled regressions are only in SI Table 3 (online). Control compliance is self-reported (90 percent reported using no digital tools, p. 6).

one_line_finding: In an online experiment that randomly assigned UK university students to use or not use ChatGPT on a 10-minute task listing uses for a 'printer that can print anything in 2097' (225 analyzed), the AI arm's mean counts of uses and of conceptual domains were above Control's in all four subgroups (Fig. 2, p. 6), with no significant difference in frequency in Group 2 (b = 0.91, SE = 2.30, p = .69) or on either count in Group 4 (p. 6), and the AI condition's pooled outputs scored higher on group-level frequency (635 vs 552) and flexibility (442 vs 313) (Fig. 5, p. 9); pooled regressions are only in SI Table 3, not in this PDF.
open_questions: Arm sizes (AI vs Control) are not in the main text; SI Table 1 is described only as a demographic breakdown.

Pooled across-group treatment coefficients for frequency, flexibility, inaccuracy and unclarity are only in SI Table 3, which is not in this PDF. The PDF prints b and SE for three within-group contrasts only.

Sample arithmetic: 266 - 43 = 223, but the paper reports a final sample of 225 and group counts summing to 225 (p. 4); the t-tests on p. 8 (df 221 within person, df 220 between arms) imply 222 people.

Where the attention check sat in the study is not stated. The 43 excluded people had completed the study, so they were dropped after assignment, and the paper does not show whether failing the check could depend on condition.
Whether randomization was stratified by the four groups is not stated; the paper says only that the selection 'ensured balanced representation across both control and experimental conditions' (p. 4).

How the group-level counts in Fig. 5 were computed is not described. They are not additive across subgroups, so they are not plain sums of individual counts, and the paper reports no scaling by arm size. SI Table 5 may describe the method.

The text on p. 7 swaps the Grp 9 flexibility and frequency values relative to Fig. 5, and the Fig. 5 caption swaps the colour wording. The figure's legend and the subgroup values quoted in the text agree with the figure's panel labels, and those labels are the only ones under which frequency is at least flexibility in every bar pair, as the definitions on p. 5 require.
Measure code for the LLM counts: category_count (a count of ideas and categories) or automated_score (a language model doing the scoring).

Outputs were scored by GPT-4o/GPT-4 Turbo, and the paper does not say which model's counts enter the analysis. It notes that 'The use of AI for rating creativity introduces the possibility of bias' (p. 11). Human validation covered 40 of the 225 responses; the human raters were blinded to group and condition.
Which ChatGPT model or tier the AI arm used, how participants reached ChatGPT, and whether any instruction limited how they used it are not stated (p. 5).
notes: One study. Not listed as outcomes: writing time (a process measure, not scored on the output; the AI arm was faster, Fig. 2); pre-to-post changes in self-reported value, enjoyment, difficulty, effort, trust and moral acceptance (Section 3.3, Fig. 6, SI Table 6); the moral-acceptance-with-transparency t-tests (p. 8); the HAI dyad comparison (Section 3.2.2, Fig. 4, SI Table 4), which groups participants by self-reported usage (Human-only, AI-only, AI-led, Human-AI-dyadic) and is not randomized; and the demographic heterogeneity analysis (Section 3.2.1, Fig. 3), which repeats the individual-level outcomes in 21 subgroups. The candidate record's 'experiment_assignment_unclear' is resolved: the paper states random assignment between subjects (p. 5; Fig. 1, p. 4). The p. 4 phrase 'randomly selected based on their English proficiency and prior experience with ChatGPT' describes the four-group labelling, which the Fig. 1 caption places before random assignment. Task coded divergent_test because it asks for as many uses as possible of a hypothetical object and is scored for fluency and flexibility; the paper calls it a creative writing task.

differences.resolved: not_stated (B). The paper never labels the Grammarly measures primary or secondary. Hypothesis 1 names writing quality beside divergent thinking, and Section 3.1 tests creativity and writing quality together as the preregistered performance outcomes.

open_items.item: Arm sizes (AI vs Control) are not printed in the main text, and the paper describes SI Table 1 only as a demographic breakdown. Criterion 2 counts all people analyzed and does not need them.
Pooled across-group coefficients and SEs for frequency, flexibility, inaccuracy and unclarity are only in SI Table 3 (online). The PDF prints b and SE for three within-group contrasts.
Sample arithmetic: 266 - 43 = 223, not the reported 225, and the p. 8 t-tests imply 222 people. Every count is far above 50, so criterion 2 holds under any of them.

Where the attention check sat in the study is not stated. The 43 excluded people completed the study, so they were dropped after assignment. The paper states random assignment either way, so criterion 1 holds.
Whether randomization was stratified by the four groups is not stated. The paper states random assignment either way.

How the Fig. 5 group-level counts were computed (removal of duplicates across participants, any scaling by arm size) is not described. Criterion 3 rests on the individual counts S1-O1 and S1-O2 in any case.

The p. 7 text swaps the Grp 9 flexibility and frequency values, and the Fig. 5 caption swaps the colour wording. The form follows the figure's panel labels and legend, the only labelling under which frequency is at least flexibility in every bar pair.
Measure code for the LLM counts: category_count or automated_score. This is a codebook decision for Review 1. Both codes are scores on the output, so criterion 3 holds under either.
Which LLM's counts (GPT-4o or GPT-4 Turbo) enter the analysis is not stated. Human validation covered 40 of the 225 responses, with the ICCs printed on p. 5.

Which ChatGPT model or tier the AI arm used, how participants reached ChatGPT, and whether any instruction limited how they used it are not stated. ChatGPT is generative AI under any model, so criterion 1 holds.
